pages.title: About The Ambiguity Project
pages.description: What The Ambiguity Project does and how we do it.
pages.body:
The Ambiguity Project is a 501(c)(3) non-profit helping people, students, businesses, governments, organizations, and schools better recognize, live with, and navigate ambiguity.

We write books, share what we are learning on our blog, and build tools that support people as they confront ambiguity in different situations.

pages.title: Ambiguity Everywhere
pages.description: Ambiguity Everywhere: shaping our lives, society, and the world.
pages.body: All of life’s experiences, from how we learn, to our relationships, to scientific progress, to the economy, to voting, and much more, are ambiguous. *Ambiguity Everywhere* explores these wide-ranging aspects of our world and how experts in each approach and manage ambiguity.

library.title: Not Knowing: The Art of Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity
library.author: Steven D'Souza & Diana Renner
library.summary: A practical, reflective guide to staying with the unknown instead of rushing to close it down.
library.body:
Where most books on uncertainty try to shrink it, this one asks what happens if you stop fighting it. D'Souza and Renner draw on leadership coaching, art and philosophy to argue that the edge of what we know is where learning actually happens.

The exercises are the best part: short prompts for noticing when you are reaching for false certainty. A quiet book, and a useful one.

library.title: Thinking in Bets
library.author: Annie Duke
library.coverAlt: Cover of Thinking in Bets by Annie Duke
library.summary: A former professional poker player on separating the quality of a decision from the luck of its outcome.
library.body:
Duke's big idea fits in a sentence: **a good decision can have a bad outcome, and a bad decision can get lucky.** She calls the mistake of judging decisions by their results "resulting", and once you have a word for it you see it everywhere.

## Most useful takeaways

- Treat beliefs as bets with a confidence level attached, not as true-or-false statements.
- Ask "wanna bet?" of your own opinions. The question exposes how sure you really are.
- Build a small group that holds you to the habit of reviewing *process*, not just results.

## Our take

It is an approachable on-ramp to probabilistic thinking, ideal for students and teams who have never been asked to put a number on their uncertainty. The poker stories carry the book; the self-help chapters near the end are thinner.
